{{Short description|Fewest cliques covering a graph's edges}}

[[File:Erdős–Faber–Lovász conjecture.svg|thumb|A graph with intersection number four. The four shaded regions indicate four cliques that cover all the edges of the graph. In an intersection representation, each vertex can be represented by the subset of these cliques that it belongs to.]]
In the [[mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], the '''intersection number''' of a graph <math>G=(V,E)</math> is the smallest number of elements needed to represent <math>G</math> as an [[intersection graph]] of [[finite set]]s. In such a representation, each vertex is represented as a set, and two vertices are connected by an edge whenever their sets have a common element. The intersection number equals the smallest number of [[clique (graph theory)|cliques]] (subgraphs with edges between all pairs of vertices) needed to [[Edge cover|cover]] all of the edges of <math>G</math>.{{r|gy06|r85}} Both this number and the computational problem of finding it have been studied under many alternative names.

Applications of the intersection number include [[scheduling]] users of a shared resource or operations on [[very long instruction word]] computers, bandwidth allocation in [[fiber optic]] networks, data visualization using [[compact letter display]]s, the analysis of [[food web]]s in biology, and the inference of [[protein complex]]es from [[protein–protein interaction]] networks.

Every graph with <math>n</math> vertices and <math>m</math> edges has intersection number at most <math>\min(m,n^2/4)</math>. The intersection number is [[NP-hard]] to compute or approximate, but [[fixed-parameter tractable]].

==Nomenclature==
The two equivalent formulations of the intersection number, in terms of intersection graphs or in terms of cliques that cover all edges, have been the sources of multiple names for this concept, and for the computational problem of finding an intersection graph representation or a cover by cliques.

A set of cliques that cover all edges of a graph is called a '''clique edge cover'''{{r|sv04}} or '''edge clique cover''',{{r|mtq06}} or even just a '''clique cover''', although the last term is ambiguous: a [[clique cover]] can also be a set of cliques that cover all vertices of a graph.{{r|gghn09}} Sometimes "covering" is used in place of "cover".{{r|a86}} As well as being called the intersection number, the minimum number of these cliques has been called the '''''R''-content''',{{r|o77}} '''edge clique cover number''',{{r|mtq06}} or '''clique cover number'''.{{r|jh19}}

The problem of computing the intersection number has been called the '''intersection number problem''',{{r|rs07}} the '''intersection graph basis problem''',{{r|gj79}} '''covering by cliques''',{{r|gj79}} the '''edge clique cover problem''',{{r|rs07}} and (because of one of its early applications) the '''keyword conflict problem'''.{{r|r85}}

==Definitions==
===Intersection graphs===
Let <math>\mathcal{F}</math> be a [[family of sets]], allowing sets in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> to be repeated. Then the [[intersection graph]] of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is an [[undirected graph]] that has a vertex for each set in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and an edge between each two sets that have a nonempty intersection. Every graph can be represented as an intersection graph in this way.{{r|sm45}} The intersection number of the graph is the smallest number <math>k</math> such that there exists a representation of this type for which the union of the sets in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> has <math>k</math> elements.{{r|gy06}} The problem of finding an intersection representation of a graph, using a given number of elements, is known as the ''intersection graph basis problem''.{{r|gj79}}

===Clique edge covers===
An alternative definition of the intersection number of a graph <math>G</math> is that it is the smallest number of [[clique (graph theory)|cliques]] in <math>G</math> ([[complete graph|complete]] [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraphs]] of <math>G</math>) that together cover all of the edges of <math>G</math>.{{r|gy06|egp66}} A set of cliques with this property is known as a ''clique edge cover'' or ''edge clique cover'', and for this reason the intersection number is also sometimes called the ''edge clique cover number''.{{r|mtq06}}

===Equivalence===
The equality of the intersection number and the edge clique cover number has a short proof. In one direction, suppose that <math>G</math> is the intersection graph of a family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of sets whose union <math>U</math> has <math>k</math> elements. Then for every element <math>x\in U</math>, the sets in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> that contain <math>x</math> form a clique <math>K_x</math> in <math>G</math>, because each pair of these sets has a non-empty intersection containing <math>x</math>. Further, the cliques formed in this way cover every edge in <math>G</math>: if two sets in <math>\mathcal{F}</math> form an edge by having a non-empty intersection, then that edge is contained in the clique <math>K_x</math> for every element <math>x</math> that belongs to their intersection. Therefore, the edges of <math>G</math> can be covered by <math>k</math> cliques, one per element of <math>U</math>.{{r|egp66}}

In the other direction, if the edges of graph <math>G</math> can be covered by <math>k</math> cliques, then each vertex <math>v</math> of <math>G</math> may be represented by the set of cliques in this cover that contain <math>v</math>. Two of these sets of cliques, for two vertices <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>, have a nonempty intersection if and only if there is a clique in the cover that contains both <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>. If this clique containing <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> exists, then it also contains edge <math>uv</math>, which must therefore be an edge in <math>G</math>. Conversely, if <math>uv</math> is an edge in <math>G</math>, then it must be covered by a clique in the cover; this covering clique contains both <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>, so it belongs to the intersection of the sets of cliques that represent <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>. Therefore, a cover by <math>k</math> cliques leads to an intersection representation with <math>k</math> elements.{{r|egp66}}

==Applications==
The representation of a graph as an abstract intersection graph of sets can be used to construct more concrete geometric intersection representations of the same graph. In particular, if a graph has intersection number <math>k</math>, it can be represented as an intersection graph of <math>k</math>-dimensional unit [[hypersphere]]s. The minimum dimension of the hyperspheres in such a representation is called the [[Sphericity (graph theory)|sphericity]] of a graph, so the sphericity is less than or equal to the intersection number.{{r|mtq06}}

A clique cover can be used as a kind of [[Implicit graph|adjacency labelling scheme]] for a graph, in which each vertex is labeled by a binary value, in a way that allows the existence of an edge between two vertices to be tested quickly by comparing their values. These labels have one bit per clique, which is set to zero if the vertex does not belong to the clique and one if the vertex belongs to the clique. With this labeling scheme, two vertices are adjacent if and only if the [[bitwise and]] of their labels is nonzero. The length of the labels is the intersection number of the graph. When this length is small, a computer representation of the graph that uses only these label can use less memory than explicit methods such as [[adjacency list]]s, and have faster tests for whether two vertices are adjacent. This method was used in an early application of intersection numbers, for labeling a set of keywords so that conflicting keywords could be quickly detected, by E. Kellerman of [[IBM]]. For this reason, another name for the problem of computing intersection numbers is the ''keyword conflict problem''.{{r|k73|ksw78}} Similarly, in [[computational geometry]], representations based on the intersection number have been considered as a compact representation for [[visibility graph]]s, although there exist geometric inputs for which this representation requires a near-quadratic number of cliques.{{r|aaas94}}

Another class of applications comes from [[scheduling]] problems in which multiple users of a shared resource should be scheduled for time slots, in such a way that incompatible requests are never scheduled for the same time slot but all pairs of compatible requests are given at least one time slot together. The intersection number of a graph of compatibilities gives the minimum number of time slots needed for such a schedule: one slot for each clique in a clique cover of the compatibility graph.{{r|r85}} In the design of [[compiler]]s for [[very long instruction word]] computers, a different scheduling problem arises: these computers can perform multiple operations in a single instruction, so the compiler should group the operations that need to be performed into as few instructions as possible, making sure that each group consists of operations that the computer's architecture allows to be combined. A small clique cover of a graph of incompatible operations can be used to represent their incompatibilities by a small number of artificial resources (one resource per clique), allowing resource-based scheduling techniques to be used to assign operations to {{nowrap|instructions.{{r|rvm00}}}}

F. B. Shephard and A. Vetta, researchers at [[Bell Labs]] and [[McGill University]], observe that the intersection number of a network equals the minimum number of constraints needed in an [[integer programming]] formulation of the problem of computing [[Independent set (graph theory)|maximum independent sets]]. In these formulations one has a variable per vertex that can take either of the two values 0 or 1, and a constraint that in each clique of a clique cover the variables sum to at most one. They argue that, for the intersection graphs of paths in certain [[fiber optic]] communications networks, these intersection numbers are small, explaining the relative ease of solving certain optimization problems in allocating bandwidth on the networks.{{r|sv04}}

In [[statistics]] and [[data visualization]], edge clique covers of a graph representing statistically indistinguishable pairs of variables are used to produce [[compact letter display]]s that assist in visualizing multiple pairwise comparisons. These displays are formed by choosing a letter or other visual marker for each clique, and then labeling each variable by the letters for the cliques that it belongs to. This method provides a graphical representation of which variables are indistinguishable: they are indistinguishable if they share at least one letter in their labels.{{r|p04|gghnps08}}

In the analysis of [[food web]]s describing [[Predation|predator-prey relationship]]s among animal species, a ''competition graph'' or ''niche overlap graph'' is an undirected graph in which the vertices represent species, and edges represent pairs of species that both compete for the same prey. These can be derived from a [[directed acyclic graph]] representing predator-prey relations by drawing an edge <math>u-v</math> in the competition graph whenever there exists a prey species <math>w</math> such that the predator-prey relation graph has edges <math>u\to w</math> and <math>v\to w</math>. Every competition graph must have at least one [[isolated vertex]], and the ''competition number'' of an arbitrary graph represents the smallest number of isolated vertices that could be added to make it into a competition graph. Biologically, if part of a competition graph is observed, then the competition number represents the smallest possible number of unobserved prey species needed to explain it. The competition number is at most equal to the intersection number: one can transform an undirected graph into a competition graph by adding a prey species for each clique in an edge clique cover. However, this relation is not exact, because it is also possible for the predator species to be prey of other species. In a graph with <math>n</math> vertices, at most <math>n-2</math> of them can be the prey of more than one other species, so the competition number is at least the intersection number {{nowrap|minus <math>n-2</math>.{{r|o82}}}}

Edge clique covers have also been used to infer the existence of [[protein complex]]es, systems of mutually interacting proteins, from [[protein–protein interaction]] networks describing only the pairwise interactions between proteins.{{r|bkv12}} More generally, Guillaume and Latapy have argued that, for [[complex network]]s of all types, replacing the network by a [[bipartite graph]] connecting its vertices to the cliques in a clique cover highlights the structure in the network.{{r|gl04}}

==Upper bounds==
Every graph with <math>m</math> edges has intersection number at most <math>m</math>. This follows from the observation that each edge is itself a two-vertex clique. There are <math>m</math> of these cliques, and together they cover all the edges, so they form an edge clique cover of size <math>m</math>.{{r|b97}}

It is also true that every graph with <math>n</math> vertices has intersection number at most <math>\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor</math>. More strongly, the edges of every <math>n</math>-vertex graph can be covered by at most <math>\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor</math> cliques, all of which are either single edges or triangles. A [[greedy algorithm]] can find this cover by removing two adjacent vertices and [[mathematical induction|inductively]] covering the remaining graph. After restoring the two removed vertices, the algorithm then includes in the cover each triangle that they both belong two, which covers any edges connecting them to shared neighbors. Any remaining edges that connect one of the two removed vertices to a neighbor, without forming a triangle, are covered by two-vertex cliques. If there were no triangles involving the two removed vertices, the edge between them is also covered by a two-vertex clique. By the induction hypothesis, the cover of the graph with the two vertices removed has at most <math>\lfloor (n-2)^2/4\rfloor</math> cliques. The two removed vertices contribute at most another <math>n-1</math> cliques, maximized when all other vertices are unshared neighbors and the edge between the two vertices must be used as a clique. Adding these two quantities gives <math>\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor</math> cliques in total.{{r|r85|egp66}} This generalizes [[Mantel's theorem]] that a [[triangle-free graph]] has at most <math>\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor</math> edges, because in a triangle-free graph the only optimal clique edge cover has one clique per edge and therefore the intersection number equals the number of edges.{{r|r85}}

An even tighter bound is possible when the number of edges is strictly greater than <math>\tfrac{n^2}{4}</math>. Let <math>p</math> be the number of pairs of vertices that are not connected by an edge in the given graph <math>G</math>, and let <math>t</math> be the unique integer for which <math>(t-1)t\le p < t(t+1)</math>. Then the intersection number of <math>G</math> is at most <math>p+t</math>.{{r|r85|l68}} Graphs that are the [[complement graph|complement]] of a [[sparse graph]] have small intersection numbers: the intersection number of any <math>n</math>-vertex graph <math>G</math> is at most <math>2e^2(d+1)^2\ln n</math>, where <math>e</math> is the [[e (mathematical constant)|base of the natural logarithm]] and <math>d</math> is the maximum [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of the complement graph of <math>G</math>.{{r|a86}}

It follows from results on the structure of [[claw-free graph]]s that, when a connected <math>n</math>-vertex claw-free graph has at least three independent vertices, it has intersection number at most <math>n</math>. It remains an unsolved problem whether this is true of all claw-free graphs without requiring them to have large independent sets.{{r|jh19}} An important subclass of the claw-free graphs are the [[line graph]]s, graphs representing edges and touching pairs of edges of some other graph <math>G</math>. An optimal clique cover of the line graph <math>L(G)</math> may be formed with one clique for each triangle in <math>G</math> that has two or three degree-2 vertices, and one clique for each vertex that has degree at least two and is not a degree-two vertex of one of these triangles. The intersection number is the number of cliques of these two types.{{r|o77}}

In the [[Erdős–Rényi model|Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model]] of [[random graph]]s, in which all graphs on <math>n</math> labeled vertices are equally likely (or equivalently, each edge is present or absent, independently of other edges, with probability <math>\tfrac12</math>), the intersection number of an <math>n</math>-vertex random graph is [[with high probability]] within a constant factor of <math display=block>\frac{n^2}{\log^2n},</math> smaller by a factor of <math>\log^2 n</math> than the number of edges. In these graphs, the maximum cliques have (with high probability) only a logarithmic number of vertices, implying that this many of them are needed to cover all edges. The other direction of the bound involves proving that it is possible to find enough logarithmically sized cliques to cover most edges, allowing the remaining leftover edges to be covered by two-vertex cliques.{{r|besw93|fr95}}

Much of the early research on intersection numbers involved calculating these numbers on various specific graphs, such as the graphs formed by removing a complete subgraph or a perfect matching from a larger complete graph.{{r|p83}}

==Computational complexity==
Testing whether a given graph <math>G</math> has intersection number at most a given number <math>k</math> is [[NP-complete]].{{r|gj79|o77|ksw78}} Therefore, it is also NP-hard to compute the intersection number of a given graph. In turn, the hardness of the intersection number has been used to prove that it is NP-complete to recognize the [[Graph power|squares]] of [[split graph]]s.{{r|lc04}}

The problem of computing the intersection number is, however, [[parameterized complexity|fixed-parameter tractable]]: that is, it can be solved in an amount of time bounded by a polynomial in <math>n</math> multiplied by a larger but computable function of the intersection {{nowrap|number <math>k</math>.{{r|gghn09|cpp16}}}} This may be shown by observing that there are at most <math>2^k</math> distinct [[neighborhood (graph theory)|closed neighborhoods]] in the graph&mdash;two vertices that belong to the same set of cliques have the same neighborhood&mdash;and that the graph formed by selecting one vertex per closed neighborhood has the same intersection number as the original graph.{{r|gghn09|g90}} Therefore, in polynomial time the input can be reduced to a smaller [[Kernelization|kernel]] with at most <math display=inline>2^k</math> vertices. Applying a [[brute-force search]] over at most <math>2^k!</math> assignments of distinct sets of cliques to the remaining vertices gives time [[double exponential function|double exponential]] in <math>k</math>.{{r|gghn09|cpp16}} The double-exponential dependence on <math>k</math> cannot be reduced to single exponential by a kernelization of polynomial size, unless the [[polynomial hierarchy]] collapses,{{r|ckppw14}} and if the [[exponential time hypothesis]] is true then double-exponential dependence is necessary regardless of whether kernelization is used.{{r|cpp16}} On graphs of bounded [[treewidth]], dynamic programming on a [[tree decomposition]] of the graph can find the intersection number in linear time,{{r|bf01|bkv12}} but simpler algorithms based on finite sets of reduction rules do not work.{{r|bf01}}

There exists a constant <math>c>0</math> such that the problem cannot be approximated in polynomial time with an [[approximation ratio]] better than <math>n^c</math>.{{r|ly94}} The best approximation ratio that has been found is better than the trivial <math>O(n^2)</math> by only a [[polylogarithmic time|polylogarithmic]] factor.{{r|gghn09}} Researchers in this area have also investigated the computational efficiency of [[Heuristic (computer science)|heuristics]], without guarantees on the solution quality they produce, and their behavior on real-world networks.{{r|gghn09|cgm20}}

More efficient algorithms are known for certain special classes of graphs. The intersection number of an [[interval graph]] is always equal to its number of [[maximal clique]]s, which may be computed in polynomial time.{{r|or81|st99}} More generally, in [[chordal graph]]s, the intersection number may be computed by an algorithm that considers the vertices in an elimination ordering of the graph (an ordering in which each vertex and its later neighbors form a clique) and that, for each vertex <math>v</math>, forms a clique for <math>v</math> and its later neighbors whenever at least one of the edges incident to <math>v</math> is not covered by any earlier clique.{{r|st99}} It is also possible to find the intersection number in [[linear time]] in [[circular-arc graph]]s.{{r|ht91}} However, although these graphs have only a polynomial number of cliques to choose among for the cover, having few cliques alone is not enough to make the problem easy: there exist families of graphs with polynomially many cliques for which the intersection number remains NP-hard.{{r|rs07}} The intersection number can also be found in polynomial time for graphs whose maximum degree is five, but is NP-hard for graphs of maximum degree six.{{r|p84|h92}} On [[planar graph]]s, computing the intersection number exactly remains NP-hard, but it has a [[polynomial-time approximation scheme]] based on [[Baker's technique]].{{r|bkv12}}
